newsitem.title: INDIA: FEATURE-Midnight freedom for India, bloody aftermath.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Midnight freedom for India, bloody aftermath.

text.p: Midnight, 15 August, 1947: Britain's Viceroy Louis Mountbatten chose this date out of the blue for one-fifth of humanity to awake to freedom.

Jawaharlal Nehru, soon to be India's first prime minister, did not believe in astrology -- but many Indians did, and Nehru told the viceroy he had chosen an unpropitious day for one of the most momentous transfers of power ever to take place in modern history.
"Never mind," said Nehru. "If you agree we can have a midnight meeting, and just before midnight strikes, we'll transfer power."
"What a marvellous, dramatic idea, that midnight meeting while the rest of the world sleeps," thought Mountbatten.
As midnight approached, Mountbatten signed the last telegrams as viceroy, and the legislative assembly was passing the resolution proclaiming independence.

At an impressive ceremony in the legislative assembly, Nehru had spoken with feeling: "Long years ago we made a tryst with destiny, and now the time comes when we shall redeem our pledge, not wholly or in full measure but substantially.
"At the stroke of the midnight hour, when the world sleeps, India will awake to life and freedom."

August 15 was a day of pomp and circumstance, of oaths being administered, ministers being sworn in, speeches, crowds, rhythmic chants of "Jai Hind" (Victory to India), the national flag being unfurled and a salvo of 31 guns being fired.

It ended with a state banquet at Government House at which Nehru toasted "King George the Sixth". Mountbatten responded with a toast to India. And at 9.15 p.m. 3,000 guests were individually presented to the Mountbattens.
MURDER AND MAYHEM

I saw more violence and slaughter in and around Delhi in the next few weeks than I had seen in Europe at war. For millions of Indians, the afterbirth of independence was a nightmare of murder and mayhem as the subcontinent broke in two -- mostly Hindu India and the Islamic state of Pakistan.

Much of the carnage was personal: Not death by bombs and bullets triggered by anonymous hands, but death visited on neighbours by former friends, by dagger, kitchen knife, meat cleaver, crowbar, brick; obscenely savage death.

The first horror stories came from the Punjab region on India's joyful day of freedom: Sikhs with kirpans (knives) ravaging Moslem neighbourhoods, murdering men, stripping and raping women before cutting their throats.
That afternoon, a train was due at Amritsar station, a makeshift refugee centre for thousands of Hindus fleeing Pakistan's slice of the Punjab.

On the eight-carriage train, the station master found a tangled heap of bodies, throats slashed, skulls smashed, bowels eviscerated. Arms, legs, trunks of bodies were strewn along the corridor. White-washed letters on the last carriage bore the assassins calling card -- "This train is our independence gift to Nehru and (deputy prime minister) Patel".

Ali, my faithful bearer, who asked for so little to squat for hours on end outside my hotel room, warned me he would have to sleep away. He risked massacre, like many other Moslem servants, by staying on duty.

I went to see Ali -- one of 100,000 refugees living in filth in a relic of Islam's ancient grandeur, the Purana Qila (Old Fort). There, and at Humayun's Tomb, another Moghul monument, the authorities had herded almost a quarter of a million Moslems.
Many of them wanted to flee to Pakistan if transportation could be found to their promised land. Without shelter from scorching sun and monsoon deluges, they lacked proper food, clothing, sanitation.

Too scared to leave the protection of the camp even to bury their dead, they threw the bodies from ramparts to the jackals. Inmates could be seen urinating, defecating, in the same water in which women were washing their cooking pots. The refugees refused to clean their latrines and the Emergency Committee had to send Hindu sweepers under armed guard into the fort.
PAINSTAKING, CAREFUL REPORTING

I impressed upon all staff the importance of guarding against inflammatory language, to cut out speculative writing and stick to official or hard and responsible sources for statistics and statements. Wild rumours circulated, which could do incalculable harm to the security of the state -- and to Reuters if found to lack credibility.

Twice daily, every morning and late afternoon, I drove myself round the worst affected areas of New Delhi and the old city, counting bodies, witnessing hideous scenes and calling at several police stations and hospitals. The killing came right up to the hotel -- that's where my corpse count began.
I was aware of the purple prose making tabloid headlines, against which my copy must have seemed prosaic and dull.
Late one night, in a move without precedent, the foreign press corps was summoned to Government House. Mountbatten came in leading Nehru, top officials and military brass.

It grieved him to say that against the reality of the violence yesterday -- 26 corpses, one or two small fires, a little looting -- a news agency, one which prided itself on reliability and an international reputation for accuracy and integrity in news, had reported to the effect that Delhi was a sea of flames with blood gushing down the gutters.
On leaving, a senior Indian Information Ministry official sought me out and said: "You realise, Mr Campbell, that His Excellency was talking about Reuters?"
"Never...impossible", I said.

It was then close to midnight. I was worried that, however falsely, such a charge could be laid against Reuters. I tried to contain concern with the knowledge that I could produce, for Cabinet scrutiny if necessary, every line of copy filed to London. But a nagging sense of unease persisted.
The next morning I told the official he had made a mistake.
"No", he said, "you are mistaken; here is a telex of the story as published in the Chicago Tribune."
I read it with disbelief. The purple passages were unfamiliar, nothing like what I had written. But there it was, signed "Reuter".

"I'm sorry, Mr Campbell," the official said as I protested. "Our people in the United States tell us the same story was in the Christian Science Monitor, the Toledo Blade and other papers. There is no question about it being a Reuter story."

I could only apologise, offer him our file of all copy transmitted to London since the violence began and initiate an immediate investigation. He accepted my word but said I need not bother to send him copy of our file to London.

I shot off an urgent press cable to the editor of Reuters in London summarising what had happened and urging him to clear Reuters with a statement which I could put to the official, his ministry, Nehru, Mountbatten, the lot, proving our innocence, demonstrating how grave an injustice had been done.

Alas, it was not to be. A Reuter dispatch had indeed sullied the columns of American and Canadian newspapers. What happened was that a whizz kid on the North American desk in Reuters seeing my pedestrian version compared with the whooped-up razzmatazz in the Daily X had decided without reference to anyone that Campbell's anodyne dispatch was for the spike and a pick-up of the Daily X's version be substituted.
But instead of pinning it on the Daily X, he put it under my byline. The sub-editor was sacked. India accepted our fulsome apology. The episode was over but it left a bad taste.
